(p-529) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Balad (The City)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I swear by this city,﴾

The discussion about this particle (al-lam) has already been given, and whether it negates the oath or emphasizes it, at His saying: ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 1]. However, here it is not for negation, because Allah, may He be exalted, has sworn by this city in another place, namely in His saying: ﴿By the fig and the olive, and Mount Sinai, and this secure city﴾ [al-Tin: 1-3]; for this city is agreed upon to refer to Makkah, by His saying after it: "and you, [O Messenger], are a resident (hill) in this city" [al-Balad: 2], that is, Makkah, as will come if Allah wills.

Al-Qurtubi and others have mentioned parallels to it from the Qur'an and Arabic poetry, which do not indicate negation, such as His saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12], although the intended meaning is "what prevented you from prostrating," and like the words of the poet:

"I remembered Layla, and passion seized me, and the core of my heart almost did not break."

That is: "and the core of my heart almost broke."

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, examined this at length in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab, Removing the Appearance of Contradiction).

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

Surah al-Balad

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I swear by this city.﴾

The apparent meaning of this noble verse suggests that He, may He be exalted, informed that He does not swear by this city, which is Makkah the Honored, although He swore by it in His saying: ﴿and this secure city﴾ [al-Tin: 3].

First: Most scholars hold that "la" here is a redundant particle (silah), according to the custom of the Arabs, for they sometimes utter "la" without intending its original meaning, but merely to strengthen and emphasize the speech, as in His saying: ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 92-93], meaning "that you follow me," and His saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12], meaning "that you prostrate," according to one of the two opinions.

This is supported by His saying in Surah Sad: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created?﴾ [Sad: 75], and His saying: ﴿so that the People of the Book may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29], meaning "that the People of the Book may know"; His saying: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe﴾ [al-Nisa: 65], meaning "by your Lord"; His saying: ﴿The good and the evil are not equal﴾ [Fussilat: 34], meaning "nor the evil"; and His saying: ﴿And there is a prohibition upon a city which We have destroyed, that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiya: 95], according to one of the two opinions.

And His saying: ﴿And what will make you realize that when it comes they will not believe?﴾ [al-An'am: 109], according to one of the two opinions; and His saying: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you: that you do not associate anything with Him﴾ [al-An'am: 151], according to one of the previously mentioned opinions.

And like the words of Abu al-Najm:

"So I do not blame the fair ones that they do not mock, when they saw the gray-haired, bald-headed old man."

Meaning: that they mock. And like the words of the poet:

"And you blame me in frivolity that I should not love it, while the one calling to frivolity is persistent, never heedless."

Meaning: that I love it, and "la" is superfluous.

And the words of another:

"His generosity refused stinginess, and hastened toward him, yes, from a youth whose killer does not prevent generosity."

Meaning: his generosity refused stinginess, and "la" is superfluous, with some disagreement about its superfluity in this last verse, especially according to the reading "al-bukhli" with the genitive case, because "la" governs a noun with the meaning of the word "la," so it is not superfluous according to the reading with the genitive case.

And the words of Imru' al-Qais:

"So no, by your father, daughter of al-Amiri, the people do not claim that I fled."

Meaning: "and by your father."

Al-Farra' cited, for the superfluity of "la" in speech that carries the sense of denial, the words of a poet:

"The Messenger of Allah did not approve of their religion, and the two best, Abu Bakr and Umar."

Meaning: "and Umar," and "la" is a connecting particle.

Al-Jawhari cited for its superfluity the words of al-Ajjaj:

"In a well of destruction (la hur), he travelled and was not aware of his falsehood until he saw the morning dawning."

So al-Hur means destruction, meaning "in a well of destruction," and "la" is a connecting particle, as said by Abu 'Ubaydah and others.

Al-Asma'i cited for its superfluity the words of Sa'idah al-Hudhali:

"Is it from you (a'anka) la lightning, whose flash seems like a pierced flame, its crest vanished?"

It is also narrated as "afa-minka" and "tashayyumuhu" instead of "afa'anka" and "tasannumuhu."

Meaning: "a'anka barq," and "la" is a connecting particle.

Among the evidences for its superfluity is the words of the poet:

"I remembered Layla, and passion seized me, and the core of my heart almost did not break."

Meaning: "almost broke."

As for Abu 'Ubaydah's argument for its superfluity from the words of al-Shammakh:

"O 'A'ishah, what is the matter with your people? I do not see them wasting the noble camels with the wasteful one."

it is an error on his part, because "la" in this verse of al-Shammakh is a negation, not superfluous, and his intent is that she forbids him from guarding his property while her people guard their property; that is, I do not see your people wasting their property, while you rebuke me for guarding my property.

As for what al-Farra' mentioned, that the word "la" can only be a connecting particle in speech that carries the sense of denial, this is generally not valid without restriction, by evidence of some of the earlier examples in which there is no denial, such as this verse according to the view that "la" in it is a connecting particle, and the verse of Sa'idah al-Hudhali.

As for what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, that "la" is superfluous only at the beginning of speech and nowhere else, there is no evidence for it.

The second view: that "la" is a negation of the statements of the polytheists who denied the Prophet ﷺ, and His saying "I swear" is a new affirmation. This view, although many scholars have held it, is not convincing to me, because of His saying in Surah al-Qiyamah: ﴿Nor do I swear by the reproaching soul﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 2], for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nor do I swear by the reproaching soul﴾ indicates that He did not intend a new affirmation following the negation with His saying "I swear." And Allah knows best.

The third view: that it is also a particle of negation. Its basis is that the act of swearing an oath includes an implicit report of the magnification of the one sworn by, so it is a negation of that implicit statement by way of kinaya (indirect expression), and the meaning is that He is not magnified by an oath; rather, He Himself is great, and He swore by it first.

This view was mentioned by the author of al-Kashshaf and the author of Ruh al-Ma'ani, and in my view it is not free from distance.

The fourth view: that the lam is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'), whose vowel was lengthened. The Arabs sometimes lengthen a fatha with an alif, a kasra with a ya', and a damma with a waw.

An example of lengthening a fatha is the words of 'Abd Yaghuth ibn Waqqas al-Harithi:

"And an old woman of the Abshami clan laughs at me, as if she had not seen before me a Yemeni captive."

The original is "ka'an lam tara," but the fatha was lengthened.

And the words of the rajaz poet:

"When the old woman becomes angry, divorce her, and do not appease her or flatter her."

The original is "tarradabha," because the verb is jussive after the prohibitive "la."

And the words of 'Antarah in his Mu'allaqah:

"It flows from the nape of a furious, swift she-camel, prancing like a stallion with a bitten bridle."

The original is "yanbu'," meaning that the sweat flows from the bone of the nape of his she-camel, so he lengthened the fatha and it became "yanba'" according to the correct view.

And the words of the rajaz poet:

"I said, when she fell upon her chest, O my she-camel, how far you have roamed from my fields!"

Here "al-kalkali" means "al-kalkal" (the chest). The lengthening of the fatha in these examples is not a necessity of poetry (darurah), since scholars of Arabic have stated that lengthening a vowel with a letter that corresponds to it is a feature of the Arabic language, and it is heard in prose, as in their saying "kalkal," "khatam," and "danaq," meaning "kalkalan," "khataman," and "danaqan."

The same applies to lengthening a damma with a waw, as in their saying "burquw" and "mu'luq," meaning "burqu'" and "mu'allaq."

An example of lengthening a kasra with a ya' is the words of Qays ibn Zuhayr:

"Has there not come to you, while the news spreads, what the milch-camels of the Banu Ziyad have encountered?"

The original is "ya'tika," because of the jussive particle. And al-Farra' cited:

"I have no acquaintance with Ni-dal; I have become like a worn-out waterskin."

And from this is the words of Imru' al-Qais:

"As if I, with a falcon of two spreading wings, swift, above me I lower my left side in haste."

It is also narrated: "a hunting one among the eagles, they lowered my left side," and "a swooping one among the eagles." Also narrated: "shimlal" instead of "shimal," and according to that there is no evidence in the verse, though the ya' narration is well known. An example of lengthening a damma with a waw is the words of the poet:

"I satirized Zabban, then I came apologizing for satirizing Zabban; you did not satirize, nor did you leave."

And the words of another:

"Allah knows that we, in our glancing at our brothers on the day of separation, are pictures.

And whenever my sight turns from wherever they travelled, I draw near and look (fa-anzur)."

Meaning "fa-anzur." And the words of the rajaz poet:

"If 'Amr intended to sleep, then rise, and tighten the wrapper that is tied."

Meaning "yarqud" (to sleep). This view is supported by the reading of Qunbul: "la-uqsimu bihadha al-balad" with the lam of initiation, which is also transmitted from al-Bazzi and al-Hasan. And knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.

(p-448) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or a needy person in misery.﴾

Its apparent meaning indicates that the miskin is clinging to the dust, having nothing, so he is poorer than the faqir in absolute terms, as held by Malik and many scholars.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿As for the ship, it belonged to poor men who worked on the sea﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], indicates otherwise, because He called them "masakin" although they had a ship working for hire.

The answer to this is needed according to both views.

As for the view of those who say the miskin is one who has what does not suffice him, like al-Shafi'i, what appears to me is that the answer is: the miskin, when unqualified, refers to one who has something that does not suffice him; when he is qualified by something that implies he has nothing, that is known from the added qualifier, not from the bare word miskin.

Accordingly, Allah in this verse qualified the miskin by being ﴿in misery﴾; had He not qualified him, it would refer to one who has what does not suffice him. So the meaning of the word in its unqualified state is not contradicted by its meaning in its qualified state.

As for the view of those who say that the miskin is poorer than the faqir in absolute terms and has nothing, the verse of al-Kahf is answered with several answers. Among them: that by His saying "masakin" is meant that they were weak people who could not repel oppressors, and they claimed they were ten, five of them disabled.

Among them: that the ship was not theirs, but they were hired workers on it, or it was a loan, and the lam is for specification.

Among them: that the name "masakin" was applied to them out of compassion for their weakness.

What appears to its adjuster, may Allah pardon him, is that these answers have no evidence for any of them, so there is no proof in them that must be relied upon. What some have argued, from the reading of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, "limassakin" with a shadda on the sin, a sound plural of "massak" meaning a sailor or a beast of hides, is clearly untenable because of the weakness and irregularity of this reading. What comes to the mind of the fair-minded is that the two verses together show that the word miskin is ambiguous (mushakkik), because its instances vary, so it applies to one who has what does not suffice him, by the evidence of the verse of al-Kahf, and to one who clings to the dust and has nothing, by the evidence of the verse of al-Balad (p-449), just as the sun and the lamp share light though they differ, and snow and ivory share whiteness though they differ.

An ambiguous word, when used without being qualified by a description of intensity, is understood in its absolute sense. This is what has appeared, and knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.

The faqir also is sometimes applied by the Arabs to one who has some property, as in the statement of Malik. Among its evidences is the words of a poet of the Numayr:

"As for the faqir whose milch-camel was sufficient for his dependents, yet nothing of his pasture was left to him."

He called him "faqir" although he had a milch-camel sufficient for his dependents.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 90, verse 2:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you are a resident (ḥill) in this city﴾. "Ḥill": in the sense of ḥāll (one who dwells or resides). The doubled verb (fi'l mudaʻʻaf) has its present tense (muḍāriʻ) come from the pattern naṣara and ḍaraba; if it is transitive, it comes from the pattern naṣara.

You say: ḥalla al-ʻuqdata yaḥulluhā, with a ḍamma (u) vowel, meaning he untied the knot. And you say: ḥalla bil-makān yaḥillu, with a kasra (i) vowel, meaning he stayed in the place, when he settled there. And al-iḥlāl (ihlāl, release) means exiting the state of ihrām (ritual consecration).

(p-530) There has been disagreement regarding the intended meaning of ḥill: is it from al-iḥlāl bil-makān (settling in a place), or is it from al-taḥallul (release), the opposite of ihrām?

Most of the exegetes hold that it is from al-iḥlāl, the opposite of ihrām, and they differed regarding the intended meaning of this iḥlāl.

It has been said: it is the making lawful of Makkah for him on the day of the conquest, when it had not been made lawful for anyone before him or after him.

It has also been said: "ḥill" means ḥalāl (lawful) for him, so that what he does in Makkah is lawful and without sin, whereas they are sinners for what they do.

And it has been said: "ḥill" means that the polytheists revere this city and its sanctity in their souls, yet they consider it permissible to harm you and to expel you.

Abu Hayyan mentioned that it is from al-ḥulūl (dwelling), al-baqāʼ (remaining) and al-sakan (residing), meaning: "and you are residing in it." End of quote.

According to the first view, it is a report about the future and a promise of conquest, that it will become lawful for him after having been forbidden, so he will fight its people and prevail over them; or it is a consolation to him, that Allah knows what they do to him and will give him victory over them.

According to the second view, it is an affirmation of the nobility of Makkah, since in it is the House of Allah, which is a great honour, and then in it is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ dwelling among its people.

What appears to me, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that this second view is the stronger, although fewer hold it; this is due to indications from the surah itself and from other parts of the Noble Qur'an.

Among them: his ﷺ dwelling in this city is in fact of great importance, and most important of it is that Allah lifts punishment from them because of his presence among them, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you were among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33]. It is as if He, exalted, is saying: this secure city is safe from punishment, and these people are safe from punishment by the grace of your presence among them.

Among them: by his ﷺ dwelling among them, he encounters hardships and bears them patiently.

In this is the finest example of patience in the face of the hardships of the call. They inflicted upon him every kind of harm, to the point that they placed the entrails of a slaughtered camel upon him while he was praying near the Kaʻbah, and he endured them patiently. They harmed him upon his return from al-Ta'if, and the king of the mountains came to him to help him, but he refused, endured, and prayed for them. They prevented him from entering his city, his birthplace, and he was patient and did not curse them; and he accepted entering the protection (jiwār) of a polytheist man. This is the appropriate reading in light of His saying after it: ﴿Certainly We have created man in toil﴾ [al-Balad: 4], and this is among its greatest instances.

So if every human being struggles in his life, whoever he is and for whatever purpose, then your struggle is worthy of esteem and veneration, to the point that an oath is sworn by it. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best.

**Allah's words: ﴿By the father and that which he begot﴾**

It has been said: "the father" (al-walid) is Adam, and "that which he begot" (wa ma walad) — it has been said that "ma" is negating (nafiyah), and it has been said that it is verbal-noun-forming (masdariyyah).

On the reading that it is negating, the meaning is: "and every great one to whom no child was born."

On the reading that it is masdariyyah, the meaning is: "in the sense of the birth, from the separation of one soul from another soul, and what precedes that of fertilization and gestation, the growth of the fetus, its shaping and formation, and the facilitation of its birth."

It has also been said: ﴿By the father and that which he begot﴾ means every father and every offspring from animals and humans.

Some scholars have preferred that the "father" is Adam and "that which he begot" is his progeny, because this fits with this city (al-balad), since it is Umm al-Qura (the Mother of Cities), and he is the father of mankind. It is as if He swore by the origins and the branches of existing things.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We created man in kabad﴾.

Its explanation has already passed at His saying: ﴿O mankind, indeed you are labouring toward your Lord with exertion, and you will meet Him﴾ [Al-Inshiqaq: 6].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 90, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He says, "I have squandered wealth in abundance."﴾ ﴿Does he think that no one has seen him?﴾ He did not specify: Does anyone see him? And who is it that sees him?

It is well known that He, glorified and exalted is He, sees him. However, the answer came coupled with evidence and enumeration in His saying, exalted is He, after it: ﴿Did We not make for him two eyes,﴾ ﴿and a tongue and two lips,﴾ ﴿and guide him to the two highways?﴾ [al-Balad: 8-10]. For whoever made for man two eyes with which he sees, and knows from him the treachery of the eyes, and a tongue with which he speaks and by which He keeps account: ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is with him a watcher ready (to record)﴾ [Qaf: 18]; and who guided him to the path, the path of giving and the path of withholding. And if the matter is such, then he will not spend a single dirham except that He, glorified is He, knows it and sees it.

(p-532) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾

An-najd means the path (aṭ-ṭarīq), and it is as has already been explained in Surah "al-Insan," after the description of the creation of man: ﴿Indeed, We created man from a sperm-drop mixture that We may try him, and We made him hearing and seeing﴾ ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, be he grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan: 2–3]. That is, the path in both respects, as evidenced by: ﴿Either grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan: 3].

The meaning was discussed there, and it will come in the surah after it, at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾ [ash-Shams: 8], which gives it further clarification, if Allah the Exalted wills.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path﴾

He has already explained what is meant by "the steep path" later, in His saying: ﴿And what can make you know what is the steep path?﴾ [al-Balad: 12], and then He detailed it.

He mentioned that everything that comes in the form "and what can make you know," its detail follows it, as in His saying: ﴿The Striking Calamity. What is the Striking Calamity? And what can make you know what is the Striking Calamity? It is a Day when mankind will be like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 1–4], and what follows.

This was also mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿The Inevitable Reality. What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 1–2].

In explaining the steep path as the things mentioned, freeing a neck (fakk al-raqaba), and feeding an orphan or a needy person, there is a direction toward the necessity of spending in truth, not what a person claims without reality, as in His saying: ﴿I have squandered wealth in abundance﴾ [al-Balad: 6].

As for freeing a neck, it is contributing to the emancipation of a slave, and independently freeing one is expressed by "freeing a soul" (fakk al-nasama).

This element of action is of the utmost importance, since it has been placed first on the ladder of ascending that steep path.

The Sunnah has also come with an explanation of the virtue of this deed, to the extent that freeing a slave or freeing a soul is equated with the freed person being freed from the Fire, each limb for a limb. There are many texts on this which Ibn Kathir cited. In this there is an indication of the true stance of Islam toward slavery, and the extent of its eagerness and aspiration to liberate necks.

Thus here it makes the freeing of a neck the ladder for ascending the steep path, and made it a freeing of the one freed from the Fire, each limb for a limb. It is well known that every Muslim strives for this. He also made it an expiation (kaffara) for every oath and for zihar (the pre-Islamic repudiation of a wife) between spouses, and the expiation for accidental killing. All of these are openings for releasing captives and freeing necks, at a time when only one door to enslavement had been opened, namely capture in war against the polytheists and nothing else. These two points have been noted earlier as a refutation of the Orientalists (al-mustashriqun) and those influenced by them, in their claim against Islam that it is eager to enslave free people.

The shaykh, may God's mercy be upon us and upon him, has already spoken on His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most suitable﴾ [al-Isra': 9], in Surat al-Isra'.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or feeding on a day of severe hunger﴾ [al-Balad: 14]. That is: in a day of hardship and hunger. Al-sagib is the hungry one. Al-Qurtubi said: Abu Ubayda recited:

"Had you been a neighbor, O son of Qays, to Asim, you would not have spent the night satisfied while your neighbor was hungry."

That is: had you been a neighbor in truth, meaning in the right due to a neighbor, this would not have happened to your neighbor.

This restriction to the state of feeding is evidence of the strength of faith in recompense and of preferring what is with God, in contrast to His saying: ﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive﴾ [al-Insan: 8], according to what preceded, that the pronoun in "their love for it" refers to the food. This is common in states of hardship and hunger.

His saying: ﴿And they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves are in privation﴾ [al-Hashr: 9]. This is the highest station of virtue in feeding.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 90, verse 15:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿an orphan near of kin﴾. The yatim (orphan) is one who has lost his two parents, or one of them. In the lexicon, however, the term has been specialized: for animals, yatim refers to one who has lost his mother; for birds, to one who has lost both parents; and for humans, to one who has lost his father.

As for "near of kin" (dha maqraba), it means "of kinship" (qara'ba), and it is specified with this because feeding him is more excellent and more fitting than feeding others. The hadith on this point says: "Charity given to a relative is both charity and the maintaining of ties (silah), while charity given to a distant person is charity alone."

The hadiths on kindness to the orphan are abundant and mutually reinforcing, and it suffices to cite his saying (ﷺ): "I and the one who sponsors an orphan will be in Paradise like these two," meaning the index finger and the one next to it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 90, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or a needy person in misery﴾

It has been said: al-miskin (the needy person, one in want) is derived from sukun (stillness) and little movement, and al-matraba is clinging to the dust.

Scholars have differed concerning the distinction between al-miskin and al-faqir (the poor person): which of the two is in greater need, and what is the definition of each of them? They first agreed that when the two terms are mentioned separately, each one includes the other, and the ruling covers both, as is the case here, where feeding applies to both together. When the two are mentioned together, they are distinguished by their definitions.

As for al-miskin, it is as mentioned above. As for al-faqir, they said it is derived from al-fiqra, which is the pit dug for a palm tree or the like for planting, as if he has descended into a pit from which he does not emerge.

It has also been said that it is derived from faqar al-zahr (the vertebrae of the spine). When some of them are taken, one becomes unable to move. According to this view, al-faqir is in greater need. This is supported by what came in the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to needy people who work on the sea﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], where He called them masakin (needy) despite their having a boat by which they earned their livelihood. It is also supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Allah, let me live as a miskin, let me die as a miskin," the hadith in full, together with his saying (ﷺ): "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from poverty (al-faqr)." This is the view of the majority, in contrast to Malik.

They have defined each of them thus: al-miskin is one who finds the least that suffices him, and al-faqir is one who finds nothing at all. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 90, verse 17:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾

This is a condition on "breaking through the steep path" (iqtiham al-aqabah) by those deeds of freeing a slave or feeding; because the deed of one who is not a believer does not cause him to break through the steep path on the Day of Resurrection, due to the nullification of his deed and his receiving its recompense in this world. And "thumma" (then) here indicates sequence in mention (al-tartib al-dhikri), not sequence in time, because belief is required to exist at the time of the deed.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had already explained the conditions for the acceptance and validity of deeds in surah al-Isra', at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer﴾ [Ta-Ha: 112], and like His saying: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its due striving while he is a believer﴾ [al-Isra': 19], and His saying: (p-535) ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer﴾ [al-Nahl: 97]; because belief is the fundamental deed that moves the servant to do good, seeking thereby reward, and especially spending in the way of Allah, because it is giving without immediate return.

The scholars have examined the matter of the deed of a disbeliever which he performed while in a state of disbelief and then embraced Islam: does he benefit from it after his Islam or not?

The preponderant view is that he benefits from it, as al-Qurtubi mentioned: "That Hakim ibn Hizam, after he embraced Islam, said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we used to perform acts of devotion (tahannuth) in the Jahiliyyah; so is there any benefit for us in them?' He, peace be upon him, said: 'You embraced Islam on the basis of the good you had previously done.'" And the hadith of 'A'ishah, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, Ibn Jud'an used to, in the Jahiliyyah, maintain ties of kinship, feed people, free captives, free slaves, and carry [people] on his camels for the sake of Allah. Will that benefit him at all?" He said: "No, for he never once said: 'My Lord, forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgement.'"

Its implication is that if he had said it, that is, if he had embraced Islam and said it, it would have benefited him. And Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they enjoined one another to patience, and enjoined one another to compassion﴾

This is a completion of their attributes. Patience is general, covering obedience and restraint from disobedience. Compassion (al-marhamah) is an increase in mercy (al-rahmah). The hadith: "Those who show mercy, the Most Merciful shows mercy to them."

The mention of compassion here is appropriate alongside kindness toward the slave, the needy, and the orphan. And Allah knows best.
